description:
Ruthin Castle stands in Denbighshire in North Wales, and its origins place it directly within Edward I's ambitious 13th-century campaign to secure English control over Wales through a coordinated network of border fortresses. Building began in 1277, part of the same programme of castle construction that produced Flint and Rhuddlan, a systematic effort to project royal authority into contested Welsh territory following Edward's military campaigns. The castle passed in 1282 to Reginald de Grey, a Marcher Lord — one of the powerful noble families granted extensive authority along the Anglo-Welsh border in exchange for maintaining royal control — and tradition holds that de Grey is the historical figure behind the 'Sheriff of Nottingham' of Robin Hood legend, a genuinely colourful footnote for a family whose documented tenure at Ruthin lasted 226 years.

Ruthin's role in one of the most consequential events in Welsh medieval history came through a land dispute between the 3rd Baron de Grey and the Welsh nobleman Owain Glyndŵr. That dispute is credited with triggering the great Welsh uprising against King Henry IV in 1400, one of the most significant rebellions against English rule in Welsh history. Glyndŵr's forces burned the town of Ruthin to the ground during the rising, leaving the castle itself as the only structure standing amid the destruction — a stark illustration of the castle's defensive strength even as the surrounding settlement was destroyed.

Ruthin's fortifications faced their most severe test during the English Civil War, surviving an 11-week siege in 1646 before finally submitting — a genuinely lengthy defence by the standards of Civil War sieges in Wales. In the aftermath, Parliament ordered the castle's partial demolition, part of the wider practice of slighting captured Royalist strongholds to prevent their future military use.

The castle was substantially rebuilt in the 19th century as a country house, becoming home to the Cornwallis-West family — prominent figures in Victorian and Edwardian high society — from 1826 to 1921. Ruthin's 20th-century history moved through further institutional uses, serving as a private hospital through the 1920s until 1950, before eventually opening as a hotel in the 1960s. The property holds Grade I listed status, England and Wales' highest tier of architectural protection, reflecting its exceptional significance as a great medieval border castle.

Today Ruthin Castle welcomes non-residents for afternoon tea, served seven days a week from 1pm to 4pm, priced at £19.50 on weekdays and £21.50 at weekends, available either within the castle's historic interior or outdoors in the gardens depending on the weather and season. This daily, clearly stated non-resident access makes Ruthin one of the more consistently open castle-hotel dining experiences in this collection, set within a genuinely significant piece of Welsh medieval and Civil War history.

Ruthin itself is one of Denbighshire's most attractive market towns, its half-timbered buildings and cobbled streets radiating out from the castle grounds and giving visitors a genuine sense of the settlement Glyndŵr's forces once burned to the ground while the fortress above survived intact. The town's own market charter dates back centuries, and Ruthin's compact historic centre remains easily walkable, making a stop at the castle for afternoon tea a natural complement to exploring the wider town rather than a destination requiring a special separate trip. For visitors touring North Wales's Vale of Clwyd, few stops combine a genuinely dramatic medieval and Civil War history with such straightforward, dependable daily access as Ruthin Castle offers.

faqs.question: Can I have afternoon tea at Ruthin Castle without staying overnight?
faqs.answer: Yes. Afternoon tea is served seven days a week from 1pm to 4pm, priced at £19.50 on weekdays and £21.50 at weekends, available either within the castle's historic interior or outdoors in the gardens depending on weather and season — explicitly open to non-residents.

faqs.question: What caused the Welsh uprising connected to Ruthin Castle in 1400?
faqs.answer: A land dispute between the 3rd Baron de Grey, then holder of Ruthin Castle, and the Welsh nobleman Owain Glyndŵr is credited with triggering the great Welsh uprising against King Henry IV in 1400, one of the most significant rebellions against English rule in Welsh medieval history. Glyndŵr's forces subsequently burned the town of Ruthin, though the castle itself survived the destruction.

faqs.question: What happened to Ruthin Castle after the English Civil War?
faqs.answer: Ruthin Castle survived an 11-week siege in 1646 before submitting, after which Parliament ordered its partial demolition, a common measure against captured Royalist strongholds. The castle was substantially rebuilt in the 19th century as a country house and later passed through use as a private hospital before becoming a hotel in the 1960s.
